newsitem.title: FRANCE: French mark their difference on NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: French mark their difference on NATO enlargement.

text.p: France, determined the United States should not set the agenda for NATO enlargement on its own, is marking its difference by seeking a big-power summit with Russia and touting Romania as a candidate for alliance membership.
Both ideas, which go against mainstream NATO thinking, are part of a wider tug-of-war with Washington over what Paris calls the "Europeanisation" of the Atlantic Alliance.
Neither appears to have much chance of coming to fruition unless the United States changes its mind, diplomats say.
"France's love of taking initiatives has run up against the unwritten rule that in the alliance the initiatives come from Washington," a former NATO official commented.

The Franco-American face-off began in December 1995 when President Jacques Chirac, in a strategic shift, decided France would return to NATO's military wing, which it quit in 1966 blaming U.S. domination, provided the alliance reformed itself.

Recognising that his predecessor Francois Mitterrand's goal of building a European defence independent of NATO would never work, Chirac sought instead to develop a strong European pillar, capable of acting alone if necessary, within the Alliance.

U.S. President Bill Clinton agreed in principle, accepting the idea of a European deputy Supreme Allied Commander who would head military operations, using NATO resources, in which the United States decided not to participate.
Chirac appeared to overplay his hand last autumn, insisting that the United States hand over NATO's Southern Command, which controls the Mediterranean region, to a European.

Washington flatly refused, citing its Middle East role and control of the nuclear-armed U.S. Sixth Fleet. France then said it would not rejoin the NATO military command unless it obtained satisfaction. Relations turned raw.
The two governments are now talking to each other -- and no longer through megaphones. But differences over NATO enlargement and relations with Russia could further complicate the dialogue.

France agrees with the other allies that the process of admitting former communist east European countries should begin at a NATO summit in Madrid in July and that Moscow, which is strongly opposed, should not have a veto over it.

The French also use identical language to other allies in saying that enlargement must not create new divisions in Europe and that a charter enshrining a close cooperative relationship with Russia should be worked out, preferably before Madrid.
France is not the only country that has its own wish list for NATO expansion, but it is alone in saying Romania should be in the first wave.
"The common belief is that the three most likely candidates are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic," Spain's Foreign Ministry spokesman Inocencio Arias said.
Italy wants its neighbour Slovenia, the most northerly republic of former Yugoslavia, to be in the first group though it is sympathetic to Romania's ambition, as is Greece.
"We realise that the chances of Romania being admitted in the first wave are not strong, but we would like Romania to be told it can aspire to membership," an Italian diplomat said.

Nordic allies Norway and Denmark are keen to win assurances that the Baltic republics -- Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania -- can eventually be admitted to NATO, although they realise it will not be in the first group, a Danish official said.
"We think the first wave should be either very broad or very narrow. We don't want the first wave to also be the last," he said.

German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe named Slovakia among the potential candidates back in 1994. But there is now a broad consensus among the allies that Bratislava's record on civil and minority rights does not qualify for the first wave.
European diplomats suggest that France's support for Romania should not be taken too literally.
"They mean that Romania deserves NATO membership but I can't imagine they think Romania will be in the first wave. It's a way of showing the Romanians they are good friends," one said.
He compared the French position with Chirac's enthusiastic declarations in Warsaw and Budapest that Poland and Hungary should join the European Union in the year 2000.
"Chirac knows it's not technically possible but it's a way of showing that France really wants them in and wants to be seen as their best friend," the diplomat said.
